The Work and Torah Teaching of the Author of the "Tzitz Eliezer": Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda Waldenberg
Introduction and Biographical Background: Family Roots and Spiritual Growth
Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda Waldenberg, known to the generations by the name of his monumental halakhic work as the author of the "Tzitz Eliezer," represents one of the most complex and influential Torah figures of the twentieth century [cite: 1, 2]. His halakhic work moves along the seam between Jerusalem Lithuanian conservatism and a theoretical and practical breakthrough on the most complex social, technological and medical questions that modernity and the founding of the State set before the world of halakha [cite: 1, 2, 3]. The story of his life is interwoven with the history of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel and with the establishment of the State of Israel, and it presents a unique life path of growth from the Torah centers of old Jerusalem to the official judicial and public leadership positions of the young state [cite: 2, 3].
Family Roots and the Period of Exile
Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda was born in Jerusalem late in the year 5676 (10 December 1915), in the midst of the First World War [cite: 2]. His mother, Rachel, was the daughter of Rabbi Nachum Ragoznitsky, who served as director of the illustrious Etz Chaim Yeshiva, while his father, Rabbi Yaakov Gedalia Waldenberg, had immigrated at a young age as a lone youth from Kovno in Lithuania [cite: 2]. Shortly after Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda's birth, his father was suspected by the Ottoman authorities of spying for the Russian Empire because he was a foreign national [cite: 2]. Because of this danger, the family was forced to leave the country in haste and to live in Aleppo, Syria, for several years [cite: 2]. When the family returned to Jerusalem after the war, his father began teaching at the Etz Chaim Talmud Torah, where the young son began his Torah education [cite: 2].
Studies and Early Scholarly Development
After his studies at the Etz Chaim Talmud Torah, Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda went on to study at the Hebron Yeshiva in Jerusalem, where he acquired the analytical Lithuanian method of study characteristic of the Slabodka school [cite: 2]. His unique talent and rapid maturation found brilliant expression when, before he had even reached the age of nineteen, while still a student at the Hebron Yeshiva, he published his first book, "Devar Eliezer" (in the year 5695) [cite: 2, 4]. This book comprised 26 profound chapters of analyses and explanations of fundamental topics in the Talmud and in the Rambam, among them complex topics such as "speech comes and cancels speech," "he is subject to the greater penalty," "words cannot be transmitted to an agent" and "a bailee who handed over to another bailee" [cite: 4]. The work won enormous esteem among the great Torah scholars of Jerusalem and marked the young author as a rising force in the world of halakha [cite: 4].
In the year 5696 (1935) Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda married Shoshana, the daughter of Rabbi Avraham Werner, who served as the first rabbi of Netanya, and a great-granddaughter of the famous gaon Rabbi Yaakov David HaLevi Zlotnik (the Ridbaz) [cite: 2]. This marriage connected him to illustrious rabbinic dynasties in the Land of Israel and in Eastern Europe [cite: 2].
Public Activity and Judicial Positions
Early in his adult life he served for a short time as rabbi of the moshav Kfar Vitkin, and was even a leading candidate to serve as the first rabbi of Kfar HaRoeh (in a candidacy in which he competed against Rabbis Shaul Yisraeli and Aryeh) [cite: 2, 5]. On his return to Jerusalem he grew very close to the Rishon LeZion and Chief Rabbi of Israel, Rabbi Ben-Zion Meir Chai Uziel, and even edited the first volumes of the responsa "Mishpetei Uziel" [cite: 4, 5]. Rabbi Uziel recognized his qualities and appointed him to head the "Sha'arei Zion" yeshiva, which he had founded [cite: 4, 5].
In the year 5711 (1951) he was appointed a dayan (judge) of the regional rabbinical court in Jerusalem, and was later promoted to the position of head of the court [cite: 2, 4]. Between 5741 (1981) and 5745 (1985) he served as a member of the Great Rabbinical Court of Appeals, a post that represented the peak of his public judicial activity [cite: 2, 4]. At the Great Rabbinical Court Rabbi Waldenberg was regarded as a supreme and exceptional expert in the arrangement of bills of divorce (gittin) and the names in bills of divorce, and his practical skill was so great that he was asked to continue arranging gittin at the Great Rabbinical Court for many years after his retirement [cite: 2]. Among the prominent disciples who grew up under his guidance one may mention Rabbi Rachamim Levi, who served as rabbi of the Nachlaot neighborhood in Jerusalem [cite: 4].
Rabbi Waldenberg won broad national esteem for his writing and rulings, and in the year 5736 (1976) he was awarded the Israel Prize for Torah literature, in addition to receiving the Rav Kook Prize [cite: 2]. He died on 30 Cheshvan 5767 (21 November 2006) at the age of 90, and was buried on Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem [cite: 2, 4].
The Literary Map and the Halakhic Network
Rabbi Waldenberg's Torah writing was marked by exceptional productivity and an enormous thematic range, from theoretical scholarly investigations to the resolution of complex technological and medical questions [cite: 1, 2]. His various works sketch the picture of a halakhic decisor of comprehensive vision, who combined enormous erudition in the responsa literature (including the Sephardic responsa literature through the generations) with a capacity for precise scientific analysis [cite: 5].
Catalogue of the Torah Works of the Author of the "Tzitz Eliezer"
Below is a summary of Rabbi Waldenberg's principal works, showing the core areas in which he engaged and the character of his halakhic creativity:
Title of the work | Period of publication | Description of the structure and core subjects | Special treatises and notable chapters
Responsa Tzitz Eliezer | 5705 - 5758 (1945–1998) [cite: 2] | A monumental halakhic work in 22 volumes, covering every area of contemporary life, from Jewish ceremonies to medical ethics [cite: 1, 2]. | Includes the treatises "Ramat Rachel" (laws of mourning and physicians), "Even Yaakov" (laws of mourning), "Mishnat Terumot" (terumot and tithes) and "Remove the Stumbling Block from the Way of My People" (the prohibition of marriage with Karaites and the removal of bones from the Rambam's grave) [cite: 2, 4].
Devar Eliezer | 5695 (expanded second edition: 5750) [cite: 2, 4] | Novellae and explanations in 26 chapters on fundamental topics in the Talmud, in the Rambam and in their commentators, composed in his youth [cite: 4]. | Deals with principles of legal conception such as "he is subject to the greater penalty," "a bailee who handed over to another bailee" and the meaning of agency in halakha [cite: 4].
Hilkhot Medina | 5712 - 5716 (1952–1955) [cite: 3] | Three volumes constituting a pioneering study of the ways of conducting political government, the laws of the army, the status of judges and the electoral system according to the Torah [cite: 3, 6, 7]. | Includes an extensive introduction by the rabbi of Jerusalem, Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank, dealing with the prohibition of drafting women into the army [cite: 3, 8].
Shevitat HaYam | 5717 (second edition: 5745) [cite: 4] | Comprehensive clarifications and halakhic investigations of the details of the laws of sailing and operating a ship on the high seas on the Sabbath, and of boarding it and disembarking from it to dry land [cite: 2, 4]. | A first practical solution to the questions of the sovereign Hebrew shipping that arose with the founding of the State [cite: 2, 4].
Ramat Rachel | Printed as part of Responsa Tzitz Eliezer [cite: 4] | Clarifications of laws and halakhic investigations on matters of physicians and medicine, visiting the sick, the dying person, rending garments and mourning, following the order of the Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah [cite: 4]. | Constitutes a formulation of an ethical-halakhic code for medical staff working in religious hospitals [cite: 4].
Hilkhot Rofim u-Refuah | Late 20th century [cite: 4] | A concentrated collection of all his rulings on matters of medicine and halakha published over the years, edited by Prof. Avraham Steinberg [cite: 4]. | Serves as a practical aid for physicians, ethicists and jurists who deal with Jewish bioethics [cite: 4].
The Network of Correspondence and Social Ties
Rabbi Waldenberg's writing shows enormous affection and mutual respect for a wide range of Torah scholars, dayanim and physicians from various and diverse circles, without sectoral barriers [cite: 4]. He conducted extensive halakhic correspondence with key figures in the rabbinic world, among them a close and special relationship with Rabbi Yisrael Weltz (the rabbi of Budapest who immigrated to Jerusalem and author of the responsa "Divrei Yisrael"), and also with the Rishon LeZion Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, with whom he sat in judgment at the Great Rabbinical Court and cooperated in clarifying questions of agunot (chained women) and intricate rulings [cite: 4]. These ties attest to the central standing he acquired as a halakhic bridge between the Hasidic, Lithuanian, Sephardic and religious-Zionist Torah worlds [cite: 4, 5].
The Decision-Making Methodology of the "Tzitz Eliezer"
Rabbi Waldenberg's decision-making methodology is based on a unique combination of profound theoretical scholarship and thorough empirical investigation of the physical and scientific reality [cite: 2, 9]. He championed the Talmudic principle "a judge has only what his eyes see," and held that a well-founded halakhic ruling cannot be issued without understanding the facts in their every detail [cite: 2, 9].
Deduction and Induction Based on Straightforward Reasoning
Rabbi Waldenberg utterly rejected the use of what he called arbitrary, forced or casuistic "belly reasoning" [cite: 9]. His rulings rested on rigorous deductive thinking, which derives new particulars from ancient principles laid down in the Talmud and by the Rishonim, alongside inductive thinking that compares one matter to another on the basis of well-founded legal analogy and straightforward reasoning [cite: 9]. When he had to decide questions that have no explicit solution in the earlier literature, he turned directly to the Talmud and to the Rambam, examining their original interpretation [cite: 4, 9].
On the question of interpreting ancient sources, Rabbi Waldenberg tended to prefer the plain meaning of Scripture and the plain meaning of the halakha, and avoided casuistry that distorts the intent of the sources, adopting the principle "words are not to be taken out of their plain meaning" [cite: 9]. At the same time, when there arose a great need to be lenient in the law, he showed flexibility of thought and strove to find original solutions that balance the strict letter of the law against the needs of the hour and the relief of human suffering [cite: 9, 10].
Clarifying the Factual Reality in Cooperation with Experts
One of the prominent characteristics of the "Tzitz Eliezer" was his readiness to rely on the determinations of professional experts who are not necessarily halakhic decisors, such as physicians, engineers and scientists [cite: 2, 9]. He regarded the opinion of professionals as a necessary condition for defining the reality to which the halakha applies [cite: 2, 9].
This factual understanding kept him from applying mistaken analogies to new technologies, and led him to develop an exceptionally realistic outlook [cite: 2]. His reliance on modern science enabled him to identify cases in which a change in the physiological reality requires a change in the halakhic ruling, something that stood out especially in his pioneering rulings in the field of medical ethics [cite: 2].
The Bioethical and Medical Revolution
Rabbi Waldenberg's work in the field of medicine and halakha is regarded by many as one of the most important contributions to halakhic thought in the twentieth century [cite: 1, 2]. His rulings shaped the public and Torah discussion of questions of the beginning of life and the end of life, providing reasoned halakhic answers to unprecedented technological challenges [cite: 1, 11, 12].
Induced Abortion and Prenatal Diagnosis
On the question of induced abortion, Rabbi Waldenberg took an approach that balances the sanctity of life against the prevention of extreme human suffering [cite: 2, 10]. Whereas certain decisors, such as Rabbi Moshe Feinstein, prohibited abortion across the board and regarded it as a Torah prohibition of murder, the "Tzitz Eliezer" presented a lenient and reasoned position [cite: 2, 10].
Rabbi Waldenberg ruled that when genetic tests (such as amniocentesis, which he permitted despite its slight risks) reveal that the fetus suffers from a fatal disease such as Tay-Sachs, or from a severe brain defect such as anencephaly (a defect in which the cerebrum and the bones of the skull are missing, leading to the death of the newborn within a short time), it is permitted to perform an induced abortion [cite: 10, 13]. He broadened the halakhic concept of "great need" and determined that the enormous mental and spiritual suffering of the parents, the desecration of God's name and the blemish to the family count as a vital need permitting abortion, and in these cases he permitted the procedure up to very advanced stages of pregnancy (even up to the seventh month) [cite: 10]. He likewise permitted women who had been raped to use emergency contraception (the morning-after pill or an intrauterine device) within 72 hours of the incident in order to prevent the development of a pregnancy [cite: 13].
Fertility Technologies and Surrogacy
The arrival of in vitro fertilization (IVF) technologies confronted the world of halakha with difficult questions of defining parenthood and lineage [cite: 11, 14]. Rabbi Waldenberg at first expressed grave concern about the confusion of lines of descent and the possibility that problems of mamzerut (illegitimacy) would arise, and even tended to cast doubt on the halakhic attribution of the child to his genetic father in cases of artificial insemination [cite: 2, 15, 16].
Nevertheless, his most precedent-setting ruling dealt with the definition of halakhic motherhood in cases of egg donation and surrogacy [cite: 15, 17]. Whereas Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv ruled that motherhood is determined by the woman who carries the genetic material (the egg donor), the "Tzitz Eliezer" determined that motherhood is determined solely by the woman who is pregnant and gives birth (the surrogate) [cite: 15, 17].
To ground this bold determination, he used an analogy to the law of "a young shoot grafted onto an old tree" in the laws of orlah, that is, a young branch that was grafted onto an old tree and becomes entirely nullified in it [cite: 17]. Rabbi Waldenberg explained that the law of reproductive organs and cells taken from the body of one woman and implanted in the body of another woman is that they become entirely nullified in the body of the host woman, who is the principal one in the pregnancy and the birth, and therefore the child is considered the son of the woman from whose womb he came into the world [cite: 17]. This approach also stood in sharp contrast to the position of Rabbi Shaul Yisraeli, who entirely prohibited the procedure of surrogacy with a gentile surrogate because of the concern of turning the seed of Israel into a gentile [cite: 16].
Determining the Moment of Death and the End of Life
In his attitude toward the patient who is about to die (goses), Rabbi Waldenberg presented a conservative and stringent position that zealously guards the value of even minimal life [cite: 12, 18]. Unlike decisors such as Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach and Rabbi Moshe Feinstein, who permitted refraining from active measures to prolong the life of a suffering patient with no chance of recovery under the category of "removing the impediment," the "Tzitz Eliezer" determined that it is obligatory to do everything that prolongs the patient's life as long as there is any independent vitality in him [cite: 12, 18].
From this outlook, Rabbi Waldenberg utterly rejected the modern definition of "brain death" as the moment of halakhic death [cite: 12, 19]. In his view, as long as the heart beats (even artificially), the person is considered alive in every respect, and therefore disconnecting a patient from a respirator in this state was regarded by him as an active act of murder with one's own hands [cite: 12, 20]. He regarded the respirator as an inseparable part of the physiological care of the patient, and prohibited stopping its operation as long as the patient's cardiac and respiratory activity had not ceased entirely and naturally [cite: 12, 20].
The Precedent-Setting Struggle Against Cigarette Smoking
Rabbi Waldenberg was among the first halakhic decisors to prohibit cigarette smoking absolutely and uncompromisingly [cite: 21, 22]. Whereas many of the sages of the generation refrained from prohibiting smoking because of its wide spread among the public and among yeshiva students, and relied on the principle "the Lord preserves the simple," which halakhically allows taking a reasonable risk accepted in society, the "Tzitz Eliezer" utterly rejected this argument [cite: 21, 22].
After receiving detailed and well-founded medical information from Dr. Shimshon Shoshheim about the lethal damage of smoking to the respiratory system and to general health, he determined that smoking constitutes forbidden self-injury [cite: 21, 22]. He applied to smoking the stringent ruling of the Rambam that one must keep away from anything that involves mortal danger, and determined that whoever transgresses this and says "I am endangering myself, and what concern is it of others" deserves to be given disciplinary lashes [cite: 21].
Moreover, Rabbi Waldenberg was a pioneer in recognizing the harm of passive smoking, and ruled that there is a severe prohibition against smoking in public and enclosed places (such as workplaces, halls and vehicles), since the smoker actively causes harm and endangers the health of those around him [cite: 21].
Laws of the State, the Army and National Sovereignty
The establishment of the State of Israel in the year 5708 set before the Torah world the need to formulate a comprehensive public and governmental law [cite: 3, 7]. Rabbi Waldenberg took up this task in the very first days of the State, and published his series of books "Hilkhot Medina" (5712-5716), which constituted a historic halakhic landmark [cite: 3, 6, 7].
His Political Teaching and the Model of Democratic Theocracy
In his book "Hilkhot Medina," Rabbi Waldenberg analyzed the desirable structure of government according to the Torah [cite: 3]. On the theoretical plane, he expressed resolute support for a theocratic regime, "the rule of the Divine," and wrote that no sophisticated democratic government can equal the excellence of a government conducted according to the eternal laws of the Torah, in which the political and the religious leader are united [cite: 2].
Nevertheless, on the practical level, Rabbi Waldenberg adopted a realistic approach that integrates democratic principles within the framework of halakha [cite: 2, 23]. Relying on the position of Rabbi Yitzchak Abarbanel, he determined that the Torah does not necessarily require the appointment of a king, but allows the public to choose the form of regime and government it desires [cite: 2, 3]. On this basis he defined the authority of elected representatives to legislate laws and impose taxes as a binding legal force deriving from the power of "communal enactments" and majority consent, a model referred to in research as "democratic theocracy" [cite: 2, 3, 24].
Laws of the Army and of War
Rabbi Waldenberg engaged in a thorough clarification of the laws of warfare and of the Israeli army in his book "Hilkhot Medina" and in the volumes of his responsa [cite: 2, 3, 8]. His rulings ranged between a demand for strict ethics of warfare and the protection of the integrity of the religious camp:
The obligation to call for peace: He ruled that there is a positive Torah commandment to approach the enemy with a prior call for peace and to offer him terms of surrender before opening war, out of the conception that the aim of Israel's fighting is to break the arm of wickedness and to establish justice in the world, and not to destroy for the sake of destruction [cite: 25].
Humanitarian laws of siege: Relying on the Rambam, he clarified the details of the commandment to leave a fourth side open when laying siege to an enemy city, in order to allow the besieged to escape, and linked this to the principle that all the ways of the Torah are pleasantness and peace [cite: 26].
Rejection of the conscription of women: Rabbi Waldenberg opposed most resolutely the conscription of women into the IDF, seeing it as a grave breach in the bounds of modesty and in the structure of the Jewish family [cite: 3, 8]. Volume 2 of his book "Hilkhot Medina" opens with a long halakhic introduction by the rabbi of Jerusalem, Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank, devoted entirely to the rejection of the conscription of women, a subject that aroused an enormous public storm at the time [cite: 3, 8].
Integrating halakha into the personal life of the soldier: In the course of his discussions of the laws of the state, he also dealt with concrete details affecting the personal life cycles of the fighters, such as clarifying the law of a bride who wishes to do work during the days of her wedding, in the case of the betrothed of fighters (Hilkhot Medina, part 2, gate 3, chapter 7, section 9) [cite: 27].
Attitude to Sovereignty and to the Economy of the State
Rabbi Waldenberg saw the establishment of the State as "the beginning of the redemption" and related to it with great festivity, frequently using the expression "our State" and expressions of joy at the great ingathering of the exiles [cite: 2, 4]. He ruled that the commandments of settling the Land and of immigrating to it received reinforcement and added obligation with the attainment of sovereignty, and explained that the gates of the Land, opened with the consent of the nations of the world, entirely annulled the historic oath "that they shall not go up as a wall" [cite: 4].
He likewise attributed a special halakhic status to the territorial conquest of the IDF, and determined that territory conquered by the army is sanctified with the holiness of the Land of Israel and is obligated in the observance of the commandments dependent on the Land [cite: 2]. He saw enormous religious value in the development of national agriculture, industry and commerce [cite: 4]. Relying on the novellae of the Chatam Sofer on Tractate Sukkah (folio 36a), he determined that working the land in the Land of Israel is itself a Torah commandment of settling the Land, and compared those engaged in it to a person who puts on tefillin, while rejecting the approach that prefers active idleness from work for the sake of Torah study in the Land [cite: 2, 4].
At the same time, alongside his joy at Israel's independence, he held a conservative and zealous position against the civil legal system of the State [cite: 4]. He defined the secular courts as "courts of gentiles," to which recourse is forbidden according to halakha, and firmly rejected the attempts to legitimize them in the name of statehood or redemption [cite: 4]. He waged a sharp struggle against civil laws that uproot the laws of the Torah (such as civil inheritance laws) and called for replacing the entire legal system with Torah law [cite: 4].
The Sociological Controversy over the Legacy and the Printing
The history of Rabbi Waldenberg's books, and especially the book "Hilkhot Medina," constitutes a fascinating chapter in the sociology of Orthodox society in Israel, and highlights the tension between state-oriented halakhic rulings and conservative family and sectoral affiliation [cite: 3, 5].
The Ideological Rift Within the Family and the Concealment of the Works
Despite Rabbi Waldenberg's positive attitude toward the State of Israel and his state-oriented rulings, his only son and kin, Rabbi Simcha Bunim Waldenberg, turned to an entirely different ideological path [cite: 2, 5]. Rabbi Simcha Bunim joined the circles of the anti-Zionist "Edah HaChareidit" in Jerusalem and served on its behalf as rabbi of the Ezrat Torah neighborhood [cite: 2, 5].
Owing to the wish to avoid social friction with the zealots of Jerusalem and in light of the different outlook of the new generation of the family, it was decided to conceal and prevent the reprinting of the book "Hilkhot Medina" (as well as the book "Shevitat HaYam") after its first edition in the 1950s [cite: 2, 3, 5]. This family decision turned the book, which had been a cornerstone of every halakhic discussion of the conduct of a state according to the Torah, into a scarce and extremely rare book, inaccessible to the general public and to researchers [cite: 3, 5].
The Struggle over the Renewed Printing of the Book and the Precedent-Setting Ruling
In the year 5765 the rabbi's son, Simcha Bunim, died, and a year later, in the year 5767 (2006), Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda himself died [cite: 5]. At the end of thirty days after the passing of the author of the "Tzitz Eliezer," yeshiva scholars and researchers from the religious-Zionist public decided to take the initiative and reprint the three volumes of "Hilkhot Medina" in one new volume, without receiving explicit permission from the author's family [cite: 2, 3, 5, 7].
To clarify the halakhic permissibility of this act, the publishers turned to the rabbi of Hebron and Kiryat Arba, Rabbi Dov Lior [cite: 5, 7]. In their question they presented the dilemma: is it permitted to print a foundational Torah book whose distribution the heirs prevent for ideological reasons known only to themselves [cite: 5, 7]?
Rabbi Dov Lior published a principled and precedent-setting ruling on the laws of copyright [cite: 5, 7]:
"If the heirs do not wish to print for reasons known only to themselves, and they have the right of heirs, yet they have no right to prevent the dissemination of the Torah of the deceased... The right of the public to study the Torah of the great ones of the generation outweighs the monetary property right of the heirs, especially when it concerns a book that shows the way to conducting the State according to the Torah." [cite: 3, 5, 7]
The Storm at the Court of the Edah HaChareidit
The republication of the book aroused the wrath of the author's grandsons, who did not content themselves with an oral protest but turned immediately to the court of the Edah HaChareidit in Jerusalem to obtain an urgent injunction against the sale of the book and its distribution in shops [cite: 3, 7]. The whole affair remained shrouded in mystery among the booksellers of Jerusalem, and gave rise to various conjectures:
Some booksellers claimed that Haredi yeshiva scholars were the ones who printed the book secretly for financial profit, but had to conceal their identity out of fear of the family and the zealous circles [cite: 3, 7].
Others raised a complex supposition (a local conspiracy theory) according to which the author's grandsons themselves secretly reprinted the book in order to enjoy the fat proceeds of the sale, but hastened to apply officially to the court and obtain an injunction in order to protect their social standing in the Edah HaChareidit and to present an appearance of an active struggle against Zionism [cite: 3, 7].
Be that as it may, the struggle over "Hilkhot Medina" illustrates how halakhic rulings and public ethics are at times caught up in sectoral power struggles, and how a Torah work may become a social and political battlefield over the identity and legacy of one of the greatest halakhic decisors of our generation [cite: 3, 5].
Summary and Conclusions
Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda Waldenberg, the author of the "Tzitz Eliezer," founded a halakhic teaching characterized by boldness, creativity and zeal for the truth, both halakhic and factual [cite: 1, 2]. His groundbreaking contribution in the field of bioethics and medicine reshaped the attitude of halakha toward modern technologies [cite: 1, 2]. His lenient positions on the question of induced abortion of fetuses with severe defects, together with his determinations in the laws of surrogacy and the nullification of organs, remain to this day a model of dynamic decision-making that seeks to relieve human suffering without departing from the traditional strict letter of the law [cite: 2, 10, 17].
At the same time, his great enterprise in the field of "Hilkhot Medina" established the "Tzitz Eliezer" as a pioneer in formulating the public law of the sovereign State of Israel, developing the model of "democratic theocracy" and recognizing the State as the beginning of the flowering of the redemption [cite: 2, 3, 24]. His conservative and forceful positions against the conscription of women and against the secular courts on the one hand, alongside his warm embrace of working the land, industry and the army on the other, present a decisor with a complex worldview that refuses to be reduced to narrow sectoral definitions [cite: 3, 4].
The stormy sociological dynamic that accompanied the dissemination of his books after his death shows that Rabbi Waldenberg's Torah continues to be a source of friction and inspiration alike [cite: 3, 5]. His broad literary legacy remains a stable pillar that shows the way to many in the rabbinic, scientific and public worlds, and sets forth a model of a halakhic decisor who is not afraid of changing reality, but investigates it and illuminates it in the light of the Torah and halakha [cite: 1, 2].
